Hydrogen

Hydrogen is numero uno. It's the first element on the periodic table of elements because it has only one proton. It's the lightest and most abundant element, making up nearly 75% of our universe.

Hydrogen has no color or smell, it's highly flammable and very reactive, so it forms part of many different compounds, the most familiar of these compounds being water. Hydrogen puts the "H" in "H2O". Infact, the name "Hydrogen" comes from the Greek words for "water" and "generate" ðŸ’§.

(The Mickey mouse looking molecules are water)

Hydrogen also puts the "H" in "pH", short for "power of Hydrogen". We use a special type of paper (Litmus paper) to test if a solution is acidic or basic. The paper changes color in the solution it's dipped in, then we can use the pH scale to tells us how acidic or basic that solution is.

The pH scale:

If a solution's pH level is lower than 7, it's acidic. You might have seen the term "pH balanced" on a shampoo bottle.

Hydrogen's about 7x lighter than air, so people used to fill airships with it. It turned out to be a bad idea, seeing that the Hindenberg airship caught fire in 1890.

Hydrogen has three isotopes: Protium, Deuterium and Tritium. Scientists are trying to use these isotopes to copy the fusion reaction in the stars so that we could have clean nuclear energy.

Helium

Helium's the second most abundant element in our universe, but we're running out of it here on earth. It's a noble gas, meaning it doesn't like to react with other elements. Infact, it's the least reactive of all the elements, and like Hydrogen, it's lighter than air and has no color or smell.

Helium gets it's name from the Greek word "helios", meaning "sun". It's named that because we basically discovered it in the sun before we found it here on earth.

Helium's produced by the decay of radioactive elements inside the earth. Since it's lighter than air and doesn't react to anything in it's path, when it reaches the surface, it just floats up out of our atmosphere and into space.

Lithium

Lithium is the lightest of all metals. It floats on water, and because its an Alkali metal It also burns on water. How crazy is that?ðŸŒŠðŸ”¥ðŸ”¥ðŸ¤¯

lithium's very reactive so you won't find it chilling on it's own in nature. We have to extract it from minerals like lepidolite and petalite. The worldâ€™s seawater contains millions of tonnes of these dissolved lithium minerals.

Lithium's also found in many foods, such as mushrooms, prawns, deez nuts and seeds.

It has a whole bunch of uses, but it's mainly used to make rechargeable batteries. Lithium-ion batteries are small but powerful, good for smartphones, laptops and tablet computers.

Large lithium batteries can power electric cars, which aren't as harmful on the enviroment as petrol-powered cars.

Lithium compounds are used in some medicines as well. It's used as a treatment for biopolar disorder and could possibly be a treatment for Alzheimer's desease too. Scientists are still studying it's effects on the brain.

Beryllium

Beryllium gets its name from this Greek word beryllos, same word they used for the mineral beryl. Itâ€™s the lightest in the alkaline earth metals gang, but itâ€™s not like the others. This stuff doesnâ€™t blow up in water, and itâ€™s way harder than most other metals.

Back in â€™32, this dude James Chadwick was messing around, shooting alpha particles at Beryllium, and neutral radiation starts coming off it. Thatâ€™s how he figured out neutrons were a thing, which, by the way, led to nuclear fissionâ€” splitting atoms.

Beryllium's got mad uses. You find it in high-speed aircrafts, missiles, spacecrafts, satellites, race car brake discs , nuclear reactors, high-end audio equipment and even computer componentsâ€”anything where you need lightness, stiffness, and the ability to keep its cool when the heatâ€™s on. Alloys with Beryllium and copper get used in springs, electrical contacts, spot-welding electrodes, and even non-sparking tools. This element's versatility showcases it's importance in modern technology.

Boron

Its name comes from borax, a mineral used in detergents, but Boron has so much more range than that. This stuff is seriously hard, it's super tough. And when you get it to react with carbon or nitrogen, it goes even harder. Some Boron compounds are among the toughest substances on the planet, second only to diamonds.

You can extract pure Boron from minerals with cool names like ulexite and kernite. Back in the day, people were so crazy for Boron that they willingly moved to Death Valley, one of the hottest places on Earth, just to mine the stuff. And, fun fact, plants? Theyâ€™re basically like, â€œGive me Boron or Iâ€™m not growing, bro.â€ It's essential for them to stay healthy.

Boronâ€™s everywhere, youâ€™re probably using it every day without even knowing. Tough, heat-resistant glassware like the ones you use for baking or maybe reheating your coffee for the fifth time, Boron makes them stronger to handle the heat. There's Boron in your TV and laptop screens, keeping them from cracking when you inevitably drop them for the third time this week. Boric acid's a natural antiseptic, gentle but effective, perfect for keeping your cuts and scrapes in check. Even everyday things like modeling clay and bouncy silly putty owe their stretch and flexibility to Boron compounds.

Carbon

Carbon is life; itâ€™s everywhere in our cells. About 20% of our body consists of carbon. You can find it in the tallest trees, the smallest bacterium, the tastiest food, and the sexiest human. Youâ€™re welcome.

Out of all the elements in the universe, carbon forms the highest number of compounds, exceeding nine million known compounds. Itâ€™s the fourth most common element in the universe and an absolute must-have for life as we know it. Each carbon atom is like a networking genius, bonding with up to four other atoms, creating everything from rings to spirals of double and triple bonds. Carbon also loves making chainsâ€”sometimes millions of atoms long. Itâ€™s the backbone of all the cool, complicated structures that make living things, like you, me, and that guy down the street.

The name "Carbon" is derived from the Latin word for coal, although coal technically consists of hydrocarbons (compounds made of only hydrogen and carbon). Coal still powers a lot of our world, but itâ€™s also responsible for some not-so-sexy things like asthma, bronchitis, and, you know, global warming. Yep, coal plants are warming the planet faster than at any point in recorded history. Warmer temperatures over time are changing weather patterns and disrupting the usual balance of nature.

Pure carbon comes in a bunch of different flavors, depending on how its atoms are arranged. For example:

Diamonds: The hardest natural substance on Earth, used for cutting other diamonds and blinding people with jewelry.

Graphite: The black stuff in your pencil that you used to write love notes in school.

Graphene: This stuff is like the Tony Stark of materialsâ€”used in electronics, energy storage, and even medical equipment.

And donâ€™t forget, carbon can also shape-shift into nanotubes and fullerenes, which are just fancy names for really tiny, really cool structures.

Carbon has three natural isotopes, each with six protons (which is what makes them carbon). The difference is how many neutrons they have hanging around in the nucleus. The most common one, Carbon-12, has six neutrons, giving it a mass of 12 AMU. About 1% of carbon atoms are like, â€œI need an extra neutron!â€ and those are called Carbon-13. Then thereâ€™s Carbon-14, which is rare â€”only about 1 in a million carbon atoms have eight neutrons.

We use Carbon-14 to unlock the past like a nosy ex on social media. Unlike its more stable buddies, Carbon-14 is unstable and slowly decays over time. One of its neutrons pulls a Houdini, turns into a proton, and spits out an electron. With seven protons, it becomes nitrogen. This radioactive decay is predictable enough that we can use Carbon-14 to date things up to 40,000 years old.

Nitrogen

Nitrogen's literally all around us, making up about 75% of the air we breathe, but itâ€™s super chill. It doesnâ€™t react easily with other substances under normal conditions, which is why we use it to preserve things. Pure nitrogen's perfect for keeping foods fresh or for labs where reactions need to be kept from happening. That air in your bag of Lays chips , itâ€™s not airâ€”itâ€™s nitrogen. Keeping those bad boys crispy. In its liquid form, itâ€™s cold as hell, colder than your ex's heart. It's used it to freeze blood and tissue samples for science and stuff.

In the nitrogen cycle, it's all about transforming from a gas in the air to a form plants can use, thanks to some bacteria doing their science magic in the soil. Plants really need nitrogen to grow, but they canâ€™t directly use the nitrogen in the air. Thatâ€™s where bacteria come into play, turning nitrogen into forms like nitrates that plants can absorb through their roots. Plants need nitrogen and we need plants, so nitrogen keeps everything running smoothly. Without it, weâ€™d be in a bit of a tight spot.

It's also found in fertilizers, explosives, and even in your body, where it's part of amino acids and DNA. Basically, nitrogen's doing a lot of heavy lifting, but itâ€™s super chill about it.

Oxygen

Oxygen's straight-up the real OG of life. Itâ€™s like 21% of the Earthâ€™s atmosphere, and it's got your back every second. It's always in the game, making sure you're breathing, breaking down sugars to give you energy, and basically keeping the whole planet running. It's making sure we can survive, burn fuel, and even make steel.

This element is a key player in water (you know, H2O), so itâ€™s basically everywhere. In your body, in the ocean, in rivers.

Oxygen's essential for burning fuel, like in car engines, and even in rocket fuel, powering those epic space launches. Combustion happens when oxygen meets fuel and boomâ€”you got fire! And yeah, itâ€™s making oxides when it reacts with other elements, but donâ€™t worry, plants got your back, making sure thereâ€™s more of it through photosynthesis. Plants are like little oxygen factories.

Fluorine

Fluorine is that one element that doesnâ€™t give a f*%#! It's the most reactive thing in the periodic table, ready to throw hands with anything that crosses its path. You think oxygen is bad? Fluorine will come at you like itâ€™s got something to prove. This pale yellow gas is so wild that itâ€™ll tear up glass, metal, and even water like, "What? You think Iâ€™m playing?" But when itâ€™s part of a compound, it cools down, gets all sophisticated, and turns into fluoride, helping your teeth stay strong. Fluorineâ€™s like that wild cousin who cleans up nice for family events.

When itâ€™s locked down in a compound, fluorine does some cool things, like teflon. That non-stick stuff you use to cook your eggs. Itâ€™s slippery, -scuse me, please me. There's also hydrofluoric acid (HF)â€”that stuff will eat through glass! And we used to have these fluorocarbons in our fridges and spray cans, but they messed up the ozone, so we had to let that go. Fluorineâ€™s always either making your life better or scaring the sh*# out of you.

Fluorineâ€™s got some legit uses, like keeping your teeth cavity-free. That fluoride in your toothpaste's a straight-up bodyguard for against cavities. And you better believe itâ€™s all up in the pharmaceutical game too, helping stabilize meds. And get thisâ€”fluorine even shows up in uranium hexafluoride for nuclear fuel processing. So, whether itâ€™s in your mouth, saving the planet, or part of some nuclear sh*#, fluorineâ€™s out here handling business.

Neon

Neon, that glowing bad boy in the periodic table. Neonâ€™s a noble gas, which means it's too cool to hang out with other elements, like a kid who doesnâ€™t play with the other kids. Itâ€™s chemically pretty lazy. Neonâ€™s found in the Earthâ€™s atmosphere in trace amounts, so itâ€™s not like you can grab it on the regular. But when you do, youâ€™re in for a colorful treatâ€”bright red-orange glow in tubes and lasers. Itâ€™s mostly known for making those signs that glow in bars and clubs.

But Neon ainâ€™t just about the strip club signs, nah, this gas be working. Itâ€™s out here making TVs and plasma screens pop, like "Yâ€™all want colors? Let me blow your mind!" And in them high-voltage indicators, Neonâ€™s all like, "You see me? Dangerâ€™s coming, back up!"

It was discovered in 1898 by the British chemists William Ramsay and Morris Travers. The name "Neon" comes from the Greek word "neos," meaning "new." Makes sense, right? It was a new find at the time.

Neonâ€™s also out here in cryogenics, freezing shit down to crazy-ass temperatures, like "Yâ€™all cold? Nah, let me show you cold!" Through it all, Neon stays non-toxic, colorless, and odorlessâ€”just quiet until itâ€™s time to glow and steal the show.

Sodium

Sodiumâ€™s that sneaky homie thatâ€™s always startinâ€™ some trouble. Drop it in water, and BOOM, you got straight chaos! Dude canâ€™t chill by itself. But it ainâ€™t all wildâ€”sodiumâ€™s got jobs, too. Keeps your muscles and nerves working right, like makinâ€™ sure you can throw hands when you need to. Too much, though, and your blood pressure's gonna be up too high.

via GIPHY

Now, when itâ€™s not out here causing chaos, sodium's got it's respectable side. In your body, itâ€™s keeping your nerves and muscles doing their thing, like a personal assistant making sure you're not falling apart, it's keeping your food flavorful, your meats preserved, and your fries on point.

Sodiumâ€™s a shiny metal, but itâ€™s also so soft you could cut it with a butter knife. Heâ€™s always rolling with chlorine. Together they make salt (the stuff keeping your fries on point, and everything tasty). Sodium's in fireworks, it has a yellow-orange glow. Itâ€™s in baking soda, sodium bicarbonate (makes your cakes rise like magic). And when sodium chloride isnâ€™t in your kitchen, itâ€™s out on the streets, meltinâ€™ ice and de-icing roads. Sodiumâ€™s versatile.

Magnesium

Magnesium is named after Magnesia in Greece. Itâ€™s hiding out mostly in Earthâ€™s mantle, but itâ€™s also chilling in seawater and tons of minerals, like serpentine. Dolomiteâ€™s another source if youâ€™re lookinâ€™ for pure magnesium.

Magnesium is super lightweight, strong, and sneaky important. Itâ€™s used in stuff like airplanes and car parts, and magnesium alloys are used in various objects, from car wheels to cameras.
